## Problem

Find the Fourier transform of the Gaussian

$$g(t) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-t^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}, \qquad \sigma > 0.$$

## Proof

We adopt the convention

$$\widehat{g}(\omega) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t)\, e^{-i\omega t}\, dt.$$

Hence

$$\widehat{g}(\omega) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} - i\omega t\right) dt. \tag{1}$$

**Step 1 — Complete the square.** Combine the two terms in the exponent:

$$-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} - i\omega t \;=\; -\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigl(t^{2} + 2i\omega\sigma^{2} t\Bigr).$$

Since

$$\bigl(t + i\omega\sigma^{2}\bigr)^{2} \;=\; t^{2} + 2i\omega\sigma^{2} t - \omega^{2}\sigma^{4},$$

we have $t^{2} + 2i\omega\sigma^{2} t = \bigl(t + i\omega\sigma^{2}\bigr)^{2} + \omega^{2}\sigma^{4}$. Therefore

$$-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} - i\omega t \;=\; -\frac{\bigl(t + i\omega\sigma^{2}\bigr)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} \;-\; \frac{\omega^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}. \tag{2}$$

**Step 2 — Factor out the $\omega$-dependent part.** Substituting (2) into (1),

$$\widehat{g}(\omega) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-\omega^{2}\sigma^{2}/2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\bigl(t + i\omega\sigma^{2}\bigr)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right) dt. \tag{3}$$

**Step 3 — Evaluate the remaining integral by a contour shift.** Set $u = t + i\omega\sigma^{2}$, so the integrand becomes $\exp\!\bigl(-u^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})\bigr)$, an entire function of $u$. Consider the rectangular contour with vertices $-R,\; R,\; R + i\omega\sigma^{2},\; -R + i\omega\sigma^{2}$ (traversed appropriately; the sign of $\omega$ only flips the vertical sides, the argument is identical). By Cauchy's theorem the integral of the entire function around this rectangle is $0$. The two vertical side integrals vanish as $R \to \infty$, because

$$\left|\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\pm R + iy)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\right| \;=\; \exp\!\left(-\frac{R^{2} - y^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right) \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \quad \text{uniformly in } y \in [0,\, \omega\sigma^{2}],$$

so the vertical contributions tend to $0$. Hence the integral along the shifted line $\mathbb{R} + i\omega\sigma^{2}$ equals the integral along the real axis:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(t + i\omega\sigma^{2})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right) dt \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-u^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}\, du. \tag{4}$$

**Step 4 — Use the standard Gaussian integral.** With $u = \sigma v$,

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-u^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}\, du \;=\; \sigma \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-v^{2}/2}\, dv \;=\; \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}. \tag{5}$$

**Step 5 — Combine.** Insert (4) and (5) into (3):

$$\widehat{g}(\omega) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-\omega^{2}\sigma^{2}/2}\, \cdot\, \sigma\sqrt{2\pi} \;=\; e^{-\sigma^{2}\omega^{2}/2}. \tag{6}$$

## Result

$$\boxed{\;\widehat{g}(\omega) \;=\; e^{-\sigma^{2}\omega^{2}/2}\;}$$

**Remark.** The Gaussian is a fixed point of the Fourier transform up to the normalization: $g$ is the density of $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$, and its characteristic function $\widehat{g}(\omega) = e^{-\sigma^{2}\omega^{2}/2}$ is the density of $\mathcal{N}(0, 1/\sigma^{2})$ evaluated at $\omega$. The product of the two variances is $\sigma^{2}\cdot(1/\sigma^{2}) = 1$, which is the precise form of the **Fourier uncertainty principle** for Gaussians, and it is the unique shape (up to scaling) for which equality holds.
